subject: Art & Design
title: The Bauhaus: Origin of Modern Graphic Design
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: The Bauhaus: Origin of Modern Graphic Design.

hook.text: A German art school that lasted only 14 years (1919-1933) shaped every design you see today.

buildup.text: The Bauhaus unified art, craft, and technology. Its motto: 'form follows function.' Ornament was stripped away.

discovery.text: It pioneered sans-serif type, geometric shapes, primary colors, and asymmetric layouts — the DNA of modern design.

twist.text: The Nazis closed the Bauhaus. Its teachers fled to America, spreading modernist design worldwide.

climax.text: IKEA furniture, Apple products, Google's Material Design — all trace their visual DNA to the Bauhaus.

punchline.text: 14 years. One school. A century of influence.

quiz.question: What was the Bauhaus' core design philosophy?
options: Form follows function — stripping away ornament to unify art and technology

details.summary: The Bauhaus school (1919-1933) established modern graphic design by unifying typography, photography, and geometric abstraction into a rational visual language.
details.whyItMatters: Nearly everything in modern graphic design traces back to the Bauhaus. Sans-serif typography, grid layouts, and the principle that design should communicate clearly rather than merely decorate all originated or were codified at this German school.
takeaways: The Bauhaus unified typography, photography, and abstraction
Form follows function became modern design's core principle
Sans-serif type and grid layouts trace back to Bauhaus teaching

faq.question: Why did the Bauhaus close?
faq.answer: The Nazi government shut it down in 1933, viewing its internationalism and modernism as degenerate. Faculty members like Moholy-Nagy, Albers, and Mies van der Rohe fled to America, spreading Bauhaus principles to US design schools and corporations. The closure paradoxically globalized its influence.

faq.question: What did the Bauhaus actually teach?
faq.answer: Students studied color theory, materials, typography, photography, and spatial design through a foundational course before specializing. The curriculum broke down barriers between fine art, craft, and industrial design, training designers who could work across disciplines.
